texts.essays-claude-student:
I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, but only if it stays an option and doesn't turn into the whole thing. Having the choice helps people who would otherwise just lose the day, and losing a day in high school is worse than most adults seem to remember.

The main reason is that life interrupts school way more than the schedule pretends. Last November I had strep and my mom kept me home three days, and by the time I got back my precalc class had moved on to a whole new section. I sat there copying notes off a friend's paper that didn't make any sense because I hadn't heard the explanation that went with them. If there had been a camera on the board I could have watched from the couch and stayed with everybody else. It wasn't that I couldn't do the work. I just wasn't in the room when it got taught, and that's a dumb reason to fall behind.

It also helps people whose situations aren't temporary. There's a kid in my grade who has seizures and misses a lot, and another girl who got so anxious about coming in that she basically stopped for a couple months. For her, doing English over a video call was the difference between still being a student and dropping out. My cousin lives out in the country and gets bused an hour each way, and if she could do one or two classes from her kitchen table she'd get that time back for homework or sleep. Not everybody's day looks the same, and a school that only works if you are physically in a seat at 7:45 is going to leave some people out.

Another benefit is that it opens up classes that a small school can't afford to run. My school doesn't offer Japanese or AP Environmental Science because there aren't enough people signed up to justify a teacher. But if six kids here and eight kids at the school across the county could take it together online, suddenly it's worth doing. That's a real opportunity we don't currently have.

I know the arguments against it. People say students won't pay attention, and honestly that's fair. During the spring when we did remote learning I had my camera off and I was on my phone half the time, and I know I wasn't the only one. Some classes just don't work that way either. You can't do a chemistry lab through a screen, and my art teacher would be miserable trying to teach ceramics over Zoom. Group projects fall apart. And there's the whole social side, because school is where I see my friends, and a year of not seeing them was rough on a lot of people.

But those are reasons to keep distance learning as a choice, not to throw it out. Nobody is saying every kid should sit home every day. If it's there for the kid who's sick, or the kid who can't physically get to the building, or the kid who wants a class we don't teach, then it's helping people without costing anything from the students who'd rather be in the classroom. That seems like an easy call to me.
texts.essays-llama3-student:
Some schools offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home by way of online or video conferencing. I firmly believe that students would greatly benefit from being able to attend classes from home. In my opinion, this option would not only be convenient but also enhance the learning experience as a whole.

One of the most significant advantages of attending classes from home is the flexibility it provides. Students who have part-time jobs, are taking care of family members, or have other commitments can easily balance their responsibilities with their education. This flexibility would allow students to complete their schoolwork on their own schedule, which would be particularly helpful during times when health issues or personal emergencies arise. For instance, students who are dealing with a serious illness or injury could continue their education without having to physically attend school.

Another benefit of distance learning is the comfort and safety it provides. Some students may struggle with social anxiety or feel overwhelmed in large classrooms, which could negatively impact their learning experience. By attending classes from home, these students would be able to learn in a comfortable and safe environment, free from distractions and pressures. Additionally, students who face bullying or harassment in school could also benefit from this option, as it would allow them to learn without fear of being targeted.

Furthermore, distance learning could also provide students with better access to educational resources. With the internet at their fingertips, students could access a vast array of educational materials, including online textbooks, tutorials, and educational videos. This would be particularly helpful for students who may not have access to these resources at school or who require extra support in a particular subject area.

Finally, attending classes from home could also help to reduce stress and improve mental health. The commute to and from school can be stressful and time-consuming, especially during rush hour. By eliminating the need for a daily commute, students would have more time and energy to focus on their studies and personal well-being. This, in turn, could lead to improved mental health and a better overall learning experience.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. The flexibility, comfort, access to resources, and reduced stress that distance learning provides would all contribute to a more positive and productive learning experience. As schools continue to evolve and adapt to the needs of their students, I firmly believe that distance learning will become an increasingly important option for students to succeed.
texts.essays-claude-plain:
I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, but I want to be careful about how I say that. I don't think every student should be at home every day, and I don't think school should turn into a bunch of kids in their bedrooms staring at a screen. What I think is that having the option matters, and that schools that offer it are giving students something real that they can't get any other way.

The first reason is that people get sick. Two years ago I had mono and I missed almost three weeks of school. I got a folder of worksheets and a note that said "see me when you're back," and when I came back I was so far behind in chemistry that I never really caught up. My grade went from a B to a D minus and it wasn't because I stopped understanding chemistry, it was because I missed the two weeks where they explained moles and then everything after that was built on moles. If I had been able to log into the class from my couch, even for thirty minutes a day, I would have heard the explanation instead of trying to reverse engineer it from a worksheet. That's not a small thing. That one gap changed my whole year in that class.

The second reason is that not everybody lives the same life. There are students at my school who take care of younger siblings, who work, who have a parent who's sick, who live forty minutes away on a bus route that gets them there at 7:52 for a class that starts at 7:45. There's a girl in my grade who moved three times last year and each time she lost weeks switching schools. For students like that, being able to attend from home isn't a luxury, it's the difference between finishing the class and dropping it. School talks a lot about meeting students where they are, and this is a way to actually do it instead of just saying it.

I do understand the argument against it. Somebody is going to say that students at home won't pay attention, and honestly, some won't. I've been in a video call for a club meeting where half the squares were black and I'm sure at least two of those people were asleep. Learning is harder when you're alone. You don't have the kid next to you saying "wait, I don't get it either," which is usually the moment I realize I'm allowed to be confused. Teachers also can't see your face when it goes blank. Those are real problems and I'm not pretending they aren't.

But that argument is against making everything online, not against making it available. Nobody says we shouldn't have crutches because walking is better. The point of distance learning is to keep a student connected to a class they would otherwise be cut off from, and being connected badly is still better than being cut off completely.

So my position is yes, but as a door, not as a replacement. Keep the classroom. Keep the teacher who can see you. And then keep a way for the student who can't be in that room today to still be in that class.

texts.essays-claude-student:
If a school is going to take part of my summer, it should at least get something out of it, and so should I. That is the whole argument in one sentence. Teacher-designed summer projects almost never get anything out of anybody. I think summer projects should be student-designed, with the teacher setting the rules for what counts as work, but not deciding what the work is.

Here is what a teacher-designed summer project actually looks like in practice. Last year my English class was assigned a summer reading packet. We had to read two books off a list of four and fill out a double-entry journal, twelve entries per book, quote on the left and reaction on the right. I finished mine in the last week of August. So did almost everyone I talked to. Two girls in my class admitted they wrote their reactions off the SparkNotes chapter summaries, and honestly you could not tell from the finished packet. The assignment was designed to make sure we kept reading over the summer and what it really measured was whether we could produce twelve paragraphs that sounded like reading. That is not learning, that is compliance, and the reason is that the packet had to work for a hundred and forty students the teacher had never met yet. When you design one thing for that many people you end up designing for the average of them, and the average of a hundred and forty people is nobody.

A student-designed project has the opposite problem, which is a better problem to have. It is specific. My friend Devon spent last summer building a computer out of parts he bought off eBay because he wanted to run a flight simulator. He learned what a power supply wattage rating is, he learned that he had bought the wrong RAM, he had to return it and read three forum threads to figure out why. Nobody assigned him that. If our school had let him write it up as a summer project he would have handed in something he actually understood, and he would have had to learn to document it, which is a skill he does not have. Instead the school made him read The Kite Runner and he skimmed it.

I know the objection. If you let students pick, some students will pick the easiest thing possible and turn in nothing. That is true. I have seen it. But that is an argument for structure, not for the teacher choosing the topic. The school can require a proposal in May that a teacher has to approve, a certain number of hours, and some kind of evidence at the end, a log, a product, a presentation the first week of September. Those are real requirements and they are hard to fake, because you cannot SparkNotes a presentation about a thing you never did. The teacher is still in charge of the standard. The student is just in charge of the subject. That division makes more sense than the one we have now, where the teacher controls both and therefore cannot control either very well.

There is also the fairness question, which matters more than people admit. Not every student can do an expensive project, so the proposal process has to accept a kid who wants to learn to cook from their grandmother the same way it accepts a kid with an eBay budget. That is on the school to handle, and it is handleable.

Summer is eleven weeks. A packet gets you one week of fake work in August. A project you chose can get you eleven weeks of real work, or at least a fair shot at it. I would rather the school bet on the second one.
texts.essays-llama3-student:
Some schools require students to complete summer projects to assure they continue learning during their break. Should these summer projects be teacher-designed or student-designed? After careful consideration, I firmly believe that student-designed summer projects are more effective in promoting continued learning and student engagement.

One reason student-designed projects are superior is that they allow students to take ownership of their learning. When teachers design the projects, students may feel like they're simply following orders, rather than being motivated to learn. By giving students the autonomy to choose their own projects, they're more likely to be invested in the process and produce high-quality work. For example, a student who is interested in coding might choose to create a game or app, whereas a teacher-designed project might not allow for such creativity and flexibility.

Another benefit of student-designed projects is that they cater to individual interests and strengths. Teachers often have limited knowledge about students' interests and skills outside of the classroom, so they might design projects that don't take these into account. By allowing students to choose their own projects, they're more likely to select topics that align with their passions and abilities. This not only makes the learning experience more enjoyable but also allows students to develop skills and knowledge that they can apply in other areas of their lives.

Student-designed projects also foster critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills. When students are given the freedom to choose their own projects, they must think critically about what they want to achieve and how they'll get there. They must also be creative in their approach and adapt to any obstacles or challenges they encounter. For instance, a student designing a project on environmental science might need to research different conservation methods and present their findings in a clear and concise manner. This type of project-based learning encourages students to think creatively and develop important skills that will benefit them throughout their lives.

Finally, student-designed projects can be more relevant and meaningful to students' lives. When teachers design projects, they might not have the same level of understanding about students' everyday experiences and concerns. By giving students the power to choose their own projects, they can create topics that are directly applicable to their lives and interests. For example, a student who is passionate about social justice might choose to design a project focused on addressing issues in their community, such as poverty or inequality.

In conclusion, student-designed summer projects are more effective in promoting continued learning and student engagement. By allowing students to take ownership of their learning, catering to individual interests and strengths, fostering critical thinking and creativity, and creating projects that are relevant and meaningful, we can create a more enjoyable and effective learning experience.
texts.essays-claude-plain:
Every June my school hands out the summer packet, and every August I watch people fill it in during the last week of break. Last year my cousin did the entire AP Environmental Science summer assignment in one Sunday at our kitchen table, copying vocabulary definitions off a website while a movie played. He turned it in, he got credit, and by October he could not tell you what a keystone species was. That is what a teacher-designed summer project usually turns into. If schools actually want students to keep learning over the summer, the projects should be student-designed, with the teacher setting the standards instead of the topic.

The first reason is simple: nobody works hard on something they never chose. During the school year we do assignments we did not pick because there is a schedule, a bell, a teacher checking in, and a grade that shows up in two weeks. Summer has none of that. There is no class period, no teacher walking around the room, no friend to ask what page we are on. The only thing that makes a person open a notebook in July is actually wanting to. A teacher-designed packet is built for a room of thirty different people, so it has to be generic, which means it is boring for almost everybody. A project you design yourself has at least one person in the world who cares about it, which is one more than the packet has.

I can give a real example. Two summers ago our English teacher assigned a summer reading book and a five-paragraph response, and I wrote mine in about forty minutes the night before school started. The same summer, on my own, I taught myself to edit video because I wanted to make highlight clips for my brother's baseball team. Nobody assigned that. I spent probably thirty hours on it, watched tutorials, learned about frame rates and audio levels, and ended up making something the coach actually used at the end-of-season banquet. If my school had told me in June that I could design my own summer project and it would count, I would have turned in something I was already proud of instead of a response paper I forgot the second I handed it in.

People who argue for teacher-designed projects usually say two things. They say students will pick something easy, and they say teachers know what content we need for the next course. Both of those are fair, and both of them can be solved without taking away the choice. If a teacher is worried about students taking the easy way out, the teacher can require a proposal in May with a goal, a plan, and some kind of evidence at the end, like a log, a product, and a short presentation in September. That is harder to fake than a vocabulary packet, honestly, because you have to stand in front of people and explain what you did. And if there is real content the next class depends on, like the formulas you need for precalculus, the school should just say that outright and keep it small, a page or two, instead of pretending a forty-page packet is enrichment.

What a student-designed project actually teaches is the thing school is worst at teaching, which is how to run your own work. Picking a question, planning your time, getting stuck in the middle of July and continuing anyway, that is closer to college and to a job than any summer packet is. A teacher-designed project measures whether you can follow directions, and most of us already proved that in May. Summer is the one time of year school could find out what we do when nobody is telling us what to do, and it would be a waste to spend it on worksheets.

I disagree with the principal's decision that every student has to be in an extracurricular activity. I am saying that as someone who is actually in two of them, track and jazz band, so it is not like I hate activities. I just think that the second you make something required, you kill the exact thing that made it worth doing.

The whole reason clubs feel different from class is that nobody is making you be there. When I show up to jazz band at 7:15 in the morning, everybody in that room chose to get up early. Mr. Dickerson does not have to beg anyone to practice because we all want to sound good. Now imagine half that room is kids who got assigned there because they had to pick something and band was the only thing that fit their bus schedule. They are not going to practice. They are going to sit there on their phone and count the minutes, and the rehearsal gets worse for everyone who actually wanted to be there. Making it mandatory would not give us more musicians, it would just give us more bodies.

Another reason is that a lot of students already have things going on after school that the principal does not see. My friend Marisol picks up her little brother from the elementary school every single day at 3:30 because her mom works until six. If the school tells her she has to join something, what is she supposed to do, leave a second grader standing outside? There are also kids who have jobs, kids who take care of a grandparent, kids who go to religious school on Wednesdays. The rule assumes everybody's afternoon is empty and that is just not true. Instead of helping those students it would turn them into rule breakers for doing something responsible.

Money matters too. People say "just do a sport" like sports are free. Cleats are like sixty dollars, and for travel stuff there are fees on top of that. Yearbook needs a laptop at home for a lot of the work. If you require an activity but some activities cost money and some do not, you are basically sorting kids by what their family can afford, and everybody will know it.

I know what the other side would say. They would say that some kids would never try anything if nobody pushed them, and honestly that is a fair point. I probably would not have done track if my science teacher had not told me I should try out. But there is a huge difference between one adult noticing you and saying "hey, I think you would be good at this," and a rule on a piece of paper saying everybody must sign up by October 1st. One of those feels like somebody sees you. The other one feels like homework.

So if the principal really wants more students involved, she should fix the stuff that keeps people out. Add a late bus so kids who live far away can stay. Get a fund so equipment is not a wall. Let students start their own clubs, because honestly the reason some people are not in anything is that nothing here interests them. Do that and I think the numbers go up on their own, and the kids who join will actually want to be there. That is better than a school full of people who are only in chess club because they had to be.
texts.essays-llama3-student:
I disagree with the decision that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While I understand the value of being part of a team or taking on additional responsibilities, not everyone is suited for or interested in these activities.

Firstly, some students may not have the physical ability to participate in sports or other physically demanding activities. For example, a student with a physical disability or chronic illness may not be able to participate in team sports, but that doesn't mean they can't contribute to the school community in other ways. Perhaps they could serve on the student council or help with library events, which would be more suitable for their abilities.

Secondly, some students may not have the time or energy to commit to an extracurricular activity. For instance, a student with a heavy course load or multiple part-time jobs may not have the capacity to take on additional responsibilities. By forcing them to participate in an activity, the school is essentially putting undue stress on these students, which could negatively impact their academic performance and overall well-being.

Finally, some students may simply prefer to focus on their studies or pursue individual interests. For example, a student who is passionate about music or art may prefer to spend their free time honing their skills or working on creative projects. By mandating extracurricular participation, the school is essentially dictating what students should be doing with their free time, which can be stifling and limiting.

In conclusion, while extracurricular activities can be valuable and enriching, requiring all students to participate is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Instead, the school should offer a range of options and encourage students to explore different areas of interest. This way, students can choose activities that align with their passions and abilities, and the school can promote a sense of community and inclusivity.
texts.essays-claude-plain:
I disagree with the principal's decision that every student has to join at least one extracurricular activity. I like extracurriculars, I'm on the track team myself, but making them a rule takes away the whole point of them and it also isn't fair to a lot of kids at our school.

The first reason I disagree is that not everybody can stay after school. My friend Dani has to walk her little brother home every single day because her mom works until six. If the school made her join something, she would either have to quit it after a week or her brother would be sitting outside the elementary school by himself. There are also kids who ride the activity bus, and the activity bus only runs on Tuesdays and Thursdays, so if the club you actually wanted meets on Monday you're out of luck. A rule like this sounds fine if you have a parent who can pick you up, but it isn't the same rule for everyone even if it's written the same for everyone.

Another reason is that some activities cost money. Being on a sports team means cleats, and cleats are expensive, and so are the fees and the team hoodie that everybody else gets. Yearbook isn't free either. Student council is free but only like twenty people can be on it, so you can't just tell three hundred students to go do that. If the school is going to require something, the school has to pay for it, and I don't think our school has the money for that, because we still have the science room with the sink that doesn't work.

The biggest reason though is that forcing people ruins it. An activity is supposed to be the part of school you actually pick. When my cousin's school made everyone join a club, half the kids signed up for chess club because it was the easiest one, and then they just sat there on their phones and the kids who actually liked chess couldn't even play a real game. That's worse than having a smaller club with people who want to be there. The teachers who run these clubs are volunteering their own time, and they shouldn't have to babysit people who were ordered to show up.

I do think the principal has a good idea underneath this. Kids who join things do feel more connected to school, and that's real. So instead of making it a rule, she could add more clubs that don't cost anything, run the activity bus every day, and have an activity fair in September so people actually find out what exists. Give students a reason to join instead of a rule that makes them. That way the kids in the club will be there because they want to be, which is the only way any of it works anyway.

assignment.name: Mandatory extracurricular activities
assignment.text: Your principal has decided that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. For example, students could participate in sports, work on the yearbook, or serve on the student council. Do you agree or disagree with this decision? Use specific details and examples to convince others to support your position.

texts.essays-claude-student:
Dear Principal Alvarez,

I heard you are deciding about the phone rule, and I wanted to say what I think before it gets decided. I believe Policy 1 is better, where we can bring our phones and use them at lunch and free periods but they stay off in class. Here is why.

My first reason is that phones are how our families reach us. My mom is a nurse and her shifts get switched around all the time. Twice this year she texted me during lunch to say she couldn't pick me up and I needed to take the late bus. If I hadn't had my phone I would have been standing outside the gym for forty minutes with no idea what was happening. I know the office has a phone we can use, but there is almost always a line at the window, and Mrs. Patel can't exactly call my mom in the middle of a shift and wait. A text takes four seconds. Also my little brother's after school program calls me sometimes when they can't get her.

My second reason is that Policy 2 wouldn't really work, it would just move the problem somewhere else. Kids are still going to bring their phones, they will just keep them in their backpacks or their sock and use them in the bathroom. Then teachers have to spend class time being detectives instead of teaching, and the office gets full of kids arguing about whether their phone was out or not. My cousin goes to a school with a total ban and he says the only thing that changed is that people got better at hiding it. A rule that people can actually follow is the rule that actually gets followed.

My third reason is that lunch is supposed to be our own time. We are in class for almost seven hours, and the twenty five minutes at lunch is not instruction time. My friend Devon and I look up soccer highlights, someone shows everybody a picture of their dog, sometimes we look up a word we were arguing about. That isn't hurting anyone. And next year we go to the high school, where phones are allowed in the halls. If we never practice putting a phone away ourselves, we just get to ninth grade with no practice at it. Learning to control it is the whole point.

I know people say that if phones are allowed at lunch there will be cyberbullying and nobody will talk to each other anymore. I understand that worry, I really do. But mean stuff gets said in a group chat at nine at night, and banning phones from 8 to 3 doesn't touch that at all. And honestly our cafeteria is so loud you can barely hear a video, people are still talking.

One more thing. If you pick Policy 1, I think the class part should be strict. If a phone is out during class it goes to the office until the end of the day, and the second time a parent has to come get it. Most kids I know would think that was fair. The part we care about is lunch, not texting during math.

Thank you for reading this, and for asking students what we think instead of just telling us.

Sincerely,
Malik Ortega, 8th grade
texts.essays-llama3-student:
Dear Principal,

I strongly believe that Policy 1: Allow students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch periods and other free times, as long as the phones are turned off during class time, is the better option.

Firstly, allowing students to bring phones to school would allow us to stay connected with our families and friends who may be worried about our safety. Many parents and guardians rely on their child's phone to get in touch with them in case of an emergency, and not being able to do so could cause unnecessary stress. By allowing us to bring phones, we can ensure that our parents are able to reach us if something is wrong.

Secondly, having phones during free times like lunch would allow us to do our homework or work on projects during that time. Many students, including myself, often have assignments that need to be completed outside of class, and having a phone would give us the opportunity to get some extra work done. This would not only help us stay organized but also give us a sense of responsibility to manage our time effectively.

Thirdly, not allowing phones at all would be too restrictive. As students, we are all different and have different needs. Some students may need to use their phones to communicate with their families, while others may use it to take notes or access important information. By allowing phones during free times, we can find a balance between giving students the freedom to use their phones and ensuring that they are not distracting others.

Lastly, I believe that allowing phones during free times would actually improve our focus during class time. Without the stress of not being able to communicate with our families or access important information, we can focus more on our schoolwork and participate more actively in class.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that Policy 1: Allow students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch periods and other free times, as long as the phones are turned off during class time, is the better option. It would allow students to stay connected with their families, do their homework, and improve their focus during class time.
texts.essays-claude-plain:
Dear Principal,

I heard you are thinking about changing the phone rule, and I wanted to write to you before you decide, because this actually affects us every single day. I think you should pick Policy 1, where we can bring our phones but they have to be off in class. I don't think Policy 2 would work, and I'll explain why.

My first reason is safety and just being able to reach your family. My mom works until 5:30 and my dad works nights, so a lot of days I have to figure out my own ride home. Last November my track practice got cancelled because of the rain and I texted my mom and she came and got me in like fifteen minutes. If I didn't have my phone I would have been standing outside the gym doors in the cold waiting for the office to open the line, because there was already six kids in there using it. The office phone is one phone for eight hundred students. That is not enough and everybody knows it.

My second reason is that lunch is our time, not class time. We aren't learning anything during lunch, we are eating and talking. Some people like to talk to their friends and some people like to look at their phone for twenty minutes because school is loud and that's how they calm down. My friend Dani has anxiety and she watches videos at lunch and then she is fine for the rest of the day. Taking that away doesn't help anyone learn more.

My third reason, and honestly I think this is the biggest one, is that Policy 2 will not actually work. If you tell 8th graders they can't bring phones, they will still bring them. They will just put them in their sock or the bottom of their backpack. Then teachers have to spend class time searching bags and arguing with kids instead of teaching, and the kids who get caught get in trouble for something they would have handled fine if the rule was reasonable. A rule that nobody follows isn't really a rule.

I know what the other side would say. Phones are distracting, and that part is true. My friend got his phone taken in math because he was texting under his desk, and he deserved it. But that is exactly what Policy 1 fixes. Off means off, and if somebody has theirs out in class, take it. Punish the person who broke the rule instead of punishing all of us who didn't.

Thank you for reading this and for actually asking us what we think. Please pick Policy 1.

Sincerely,
An 8th grade student

assignment.name: Cell phones at school
assignment.text:

texts.essays-claude-student:
Dear Principal Vasquez,

I heard you are thinking about making a rule that you have to have a B average to play sports or be in activities. I want to tell you why I think that is a bad idea, and I hope you will read this whole thing even though a lot of kids are probably writing you letters right now.

My first reason is that a lot of us are already getting C's and we are still trying. My friend Devin has a C in science because he missed two weeks when he had mono and the makeup work buried him. He is not lazy. He is on the wrestling team and coach says he is one of the hardest workers there. If this rule was already in place he would of been cut from the team for being sick, which doesn't seem fair at all. There are kids who have to babysit their little brothers and sisters after school, or their parents work nights, and their grades show that, not how smart they are.

My second reason is that sports are the thing that makes some people come to school. I know that sounds dramatic but it is true. If you take away the one class period where a kid feels good at something, I really don't think their grades are going to magically go up. They will probably just go down more, because now they don't care. My cousin went to a school where they had a rule kind of like this and the kid he knew who got cut from basketball just started skipping. That is the opposite of what you want.

Also, and this is my third reason, C is passing. If a C was so terrible you would fail people for it. You can't tell us all year that a C means you are doing okay and then turn around and say a C means you are not good enough to be on the team. It's like the school is using two different rules at the same time depending on what is convenient.

I do understand why you want this. Grades matter and some people probably do let practice take over everything else. So instead of a big rule that cuts people, what if there was study hall before practice, or you have to show your coach a grade check every two weeks, and if your grades drop you get a tutor instead of getting cut? That way you still push people to do better but you don't take away the thing they love.

Thank you for asking us what we think. Most schools don't do that.

Sincerely,
Marcus Ellison
Grade 8
texts.essays-llama3-student:
Dear Principal,

I strongly believe that requiring students to have at least a grade B average to participate in sports or other activities is not the best idea. I understand that you want students to take their education seriously, but I think this policy would have negative effects on many students.

First of all, many students in our school struggle to achieve a grade B average. In fact, I know a lot of students who work really hard and try their best, but still can't seem to get a B average. If this policy were implemented, these students would be excluded from participating in sports or activities that they love and that help them develop important skills like teamwork, communication, and discipline. This could lead to a lack of motivation and even lower grades, which would be a vicious cycle.

Another concern I have is that this policy would create an unfair advantage for students who are already naturally good students. Those students who are already getting As and Bs would have an easy time meeting the new requirement, while students who are struggling to get a C average would be at a disadvantage. This would create a divide between students who are naturally more academic and those who are not. In an environment where we're supposed to be promoting inclusivity and equality, this policy would be a step backward.

Furthermore, I think that focusing solely on grades is not the best way to measure a student's worth or abilities. There are many students who are amazing athletes, artists, or leaders, but may not be the most book-smart. Should we really be excluding them from participating in activities that help them grow and develop as people just because they're not meeting a certain grade average? I don't think so.

Finally, I think that this policy would take away from the spirit of teamwork and camaraderie that comes with participating in sports and activities. When we're all working together towards a common goal, we learn to rely on each other, support each other, and grow as individuals. If this policy were implemented, it would create a sense of competition and individualism that would go against the very purpose of these activities.

In conclusion, I don't think requiring at least a grade B average to participate in sports or other activities is the right decision. I think it would be unfair to students who are struggling, create an advantage for those who are already naturally good students, and take away from the spirit of teamwork and camaraderie. I hope you will consider the negative effects this policy would have and choose a different approach to encourage students to take their education seriously.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]
texts.essays-claude-plain:
Dear Principal,

Thank you for asking us what we think before you decide. I heard that you are thinking about making a rule that a student has to have a B average to play sports or be in activities. I want to say that I am against this rule, and I have reasons.

My first reason is that a C is a passing grade. If a C was really so terrible, then the school would not pass people who get one. Right now if you have a C it means you did the work and you understood a decent amount of it, maybe not perfectly, but you passed. Telling a student with a C that they cannot play soccer is basically treating a passing grade like a failing grade, and that does not seem fair to me.

My second reason, and this is the big one, is that for a lot of kids the activity is the only thing keeping them here. I have a friend on my basketball team, I will not say his name, but he has told me more than once that he would not even come to school some days if there was not practice after. His grades are Cs and one D that he brought up. If you take basketball away from him he is not going to suddenly sit down and study more. He is going to stop caring, and his grades are going to get worse, not better. So the rule would do the exact opposite of what you want it to do.

Another reason is that being in a sport actually helps your grades. It sounds backwards but it is true. When I am in season I have practice until 5:30, so I know I have to get my homework done at lunch and in study hall or it will not get done at all. When I am not in season I have all this free time and I waste it, and then it is 10:00 at night and I have not started my science. Coaches also check grades and make you sit out if you are failing, so there is already a system, it just uses a lower line than a B.

I understand your side too. School should come first, and nobody should be playing five games a week while failing three classes. But there is a difference between making sure someone is doing okay and taking their team away from them. One is helping and the other is punishing.

So instead of a B average, maybe the rule could be that you cannot have any Fs, and if you have a D you have to go to tutoring one day a week to stay on the team. That way students get help but they do not lose the thing that makes them want to be here.

Thank you for listening to students about this.

Sincerely,
An eighth grade student

assignment.text:
Your principal is considering changing school policy so that students may not participate in sports or other activities unless they have at least a grade B average. Many students have a grade C average. 
She would like to hear the students' views on this possible policy change. Write a letter to your principal arguing for or against requiring at least a grade B average to participate in sports or other activities. Be sure to support your arguments with specific reasons.

texts.essays-claude-student:
When you have a hard choice to make, the easiest thing to do is ask one person you trust and then just do whatever they tell you. I have done that before and sometimes it works out fine. But I think most of the time it is smarter to ask a few different people first, because one person can only tell you what they know, and no one person knows everything.

Last year I had to decide if I was going to keep playing soccer or switch to running track in the spring. The first person I asked was my dad, and he said stay with soccer because I had already been playing for six years and it would be a waste to quit now. That sounded true when he said it. But my dad was mostly thinking about the money we had already spent on club fees and cleats, and he was not thinking about the part where I was riding home from practice in a bad mood almost every day. So then I asked my older cousin, who ran track in high school, and she told me about what practice is actually like, that it is way more running than people think and that the meets take up your whole Saturday. That was information my dad did not have. Then I asked my P.E. teacher and she said something neither of them said, which was that I could do track for one season and go back to soccer the next year if I hated it. Nobody had told me it was not permanent. That one sentence changed my whole decision.

That is the main reason multiple opinions help. Each person is standing in a different spot, so they see a different part of the problem. My dad saw the money and the history. My cousin saw what the actual day to day would feel like. My teacher saw the option I did not even know existed. If I had only asked one of them, I would have only gotten one slice of it and I would have thought that slice was the whole thing.

Another reason is that people have their own opinions mixed into their advice, and you can usually only notice that when you compare. My dad hates quitting. He just does. If two or three other people had also said stay with soccer, then I would know it was really about soccer and not about my dad and quitting. When only one person says something, you cannot tell the difference between good advice and that person's personal thing. Getting more opinions is kind of like checking your answer on a math problem a second way. If you get the same answer both times, you feel a lot more sure.

Asking more people also stops you from only hearing what you want to hear. It is really easy to go to the friend who you already know will say yes. My friend Marco wanted to skip his sister's recital to go to a party, and he asked three people, but they were all the people who were going to the party. Of course they told him to come. He did not ask anybody who would have said something he did not want to hear, so he basically got one opinion said three times. That shows that it is not just the number of people, it is whether they are actually different from each other.

I do think there is a limit. If you ask fifteen people you will just get confused, and then you are letting other people decide for you instead of deciding yourself. The advice is supposed to give you more information, not replace your own brain. In the end I was the one who had to run the 800 or not.

But talking to a few different people with different experiences is almost always better than talking to one. You end up seeing more sides of the choice, you can tell the difference between real advice and somebody's personal opinion, and sometimes you find out about an option you never knew you had. I ran track, by the way, and I came in almost last in my first meet, but I was glad I asked around before I decided.
texts.essays-llama3-student:
Seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice by providing a diverse range of perspectives and ideas. When a person asks for advice, they may only get one perspective, which might not be the best or most suitable for their situation. By talking to multiple people, they can get a variety of opinions, which can help them see the situation from different angles and make a more informed decision.

For example, let's say someone is trying to decide which college to attend. If they only ask one person, they might get a biased view. For instance, if they ask their friend who is attending that college, they might get a glowing review because their friend wants them to join them. But if they ask multiple people, they might get a more balanced view. They might find that some people love the college, while others have had negative experiences. This can help them make a more informed decision, taking into account the pros and cons of each college.

Another benefit of seeking multiple opinions is that it can help a person identify potential pitfalls or issues that they might not have considered on their own. Let's say someone is thinking of quitting their part-time job to focus on a hobby. If they only ask one person, they might get advice that is not considering the potential financial implications of quitting. But if they ask multiple people, they might get advice from someone who has quit a job and struggled financially, which could help them make a more thoughtful decision.

Seeking multiple opinions can also help a person feel more confident in their decision. When they get a variety of perspectives, they can see that different people have different opinions, which can help them feel more comfortable with their choice. For instance, if someone is trying to decide whether to take a risk and start their own business, they might get different advice from different people. Some might be encouraging and say, "You should go for it!" while others might be more cautious and say, "You're taking a big risk." By getting multiple opinions, the person can see that there is no one "right" answer, which can help them feel more confident in their decision.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions can be a valuable way to make a better choice. By getting a variety of perspectives and ideas, a person can make a more informed decision, identify potential pitfalls or issues, and feel more confident in their choice.
texts.essays-claude-plain:
When you have a hard decision to make, asking one person for advice is better than asking nobody, but asking a few people is usually better than asking one. I think this is true because no single person knows everything, and every person you ask has their own experience and their own blind spots. When you put all of those answers next to each other, you start to see the whole picture instead of one corner of it.

The first reason is that one person only knows what has happened to them. Last year I couldn't decide if I should try out for basketball or stay in band, because both of them practice after school on the same days. I asked my older brother first, and he told me to do basketball, no question. But my brother has played basketball since he was six. Of course he said basketball. That is the only thing he knows. When I asked my band teacher, she told me something my brother never would have thought of, which is that there is a jazz band in high school that you can only get into if you have been playing for a few years. She wasn't trying to sell me on band either, she just knew a fact that my brother didn't know. Then I asked my mom and she brought up money, because basketball needs shoes and tournament fees. Three people, three completely different pieces of information. If I had only asked my brother I would have made my choice with about a third of the facts.

Another reason is that hearing different opinions makes you figure out what you actually want. This sounds backwards but it really works. When two people tell you opposite things, you can't just copy an answer anymore, you have to actually think. My cousin was trying to decide whether to go to a school farther away that had a better science program. Her dad said go, her best friend said stay. She told me that when everybody agreed she just went along with it, but when they disagreed she finally sat down and asked herself which reasons sounded right to her. She ended up going, but the point is she made the decision instead of just following someone.

Multiple opinions also protect you from someone who is wrong or who has a reason to push you a certain way. People don't always give bad advice on purpose. Sometimes they just remember something wrong, or they want you to pick what is easier for them. If a friend tells you a teacher gives impossible tests, and then three other people tell you that teacher is actually their favorite, you know the first person probably just had a bad semester. One opinion can be an accident. A pattern is harder to fake. Doctors work like this too. If someone gets told they need surgery, people always say to get a second opinion, and that is not because doctors are dishonest, it's because medicine is complicated and two experts can look at the same scan and read it differently.

I do think there is a limit though. If you ask twenty people you will just get confused and never decide anything, and some people start asking more and more people because they are hoping somebody will finally tell them what they already want to hear. That isn't really asking for advice, that's shopping for permission. The point of asking a few people is to collect information and see it from different sides, and then you still have to be the one who chooses.

So asking more than one person helps because it gives you facts that one person couldn't give you, it makes you think for yourself instead of copying, and it shows you when an opinion is just one person's bad experience. In the end it is still your choice, but it's a lot better to make that choice knowing three things instead of one.

assignment.name: Seeking multiple opinions
assignment.text: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.

texts.essays-claude-student:
Dear Principal Nolan,

I heard you are deciding whether all students have to do community service, and I wanted to tell you what I think before you decide. I think you should require it, but the number of hours should be small, and the school should count things students are already doing.

The main reason I am for it is that a lot of people would help out if somebody pushed them, but nobody ever does. That was me. My friend Marisol tutors second graders at the library on Tuesdays and she asked me to come with her probably ten times, and every single time I said "yeah, next week." I never went. Then in August my cousin's soccer team needed someone to run the snack table and I basically got volunteered by my mom, and it was fine. It was actually kind of fun and one of the little kids kept calling me coach. I am not a coach. My point is I needed a push and a requirement is a push.

The other reason is that you learn stuff you cannot learn sitting in a classroom. When my youth group cleaned up the creek behind Miller Road we pulled out eleven tires. Eleven tires. Before that day if you said "litter" I would have pictured a candy wrapper on the sidewalk, not somebody driving down there and rolling tires into a creek on purpose. No worksheet about pollution was going to teach me that. And Devon, who tutors, told me he did not really get fractions until he had to explain them to a third grader who kept asking why, which I think shows the person helping gets something out of it too.

But I want to be fair to my friends who are against it, because people act like they are just lazy and they are not. Aisha has swim practice at 5:30 in the morning and again after school, and on Thursdays she watches her little brother because her mom works late. If you tell her she owes the school fifty hours, she is going to be doing homework at midnight, or she is going to write down hours she did not do, and then nobody actually got helped and she just learned how to lie on a form. That is the opposite of the point. So I think ten hours a year is enough. That is less than one hour a month.

Also, please count what people already do. Some kids volunteer at their church, some help out at their family's store on weekends, some babysit for the neighbors for free every Saturday. If none of that counts because there was no adult to sign a paper, then the rule is not really about helping the community anymore, it is about paperwork, and students will see right through it.

So my position is yes, require community service, but keep it small and count the real stuff. Thank you for reading this and for asking students before you decide.

Sincerely,
Jordan Vasquez, 8th grade
texts.essays-llama3-student:
Dear Principal,

I think students should be required to perform community service. I know that some people might think it's taking away from their free time, but I believe it's an important part of being a good citizen and a responsible person.

First of all, community service helps people in need. For example, my friend Sarah tutors elementary school kids who are struggling with their reading and math skills. It's making a big difference in their lives and giving them a chance to succeed. Without community service, these kids might not have anyone to turn to for help.

Secondly, community service teaches us valuable skills like responsibility, teamwork, and communication. When we work together to make a difference, we learn to rely on each other and trust each other. These skills are important for our future success, whether we're going to college or getting a job.

Lastly, community service shows us that we're not just individuals, but part of a bigger community. When we take care of our community, we're taking care of ourselves. It's a way to give back for all the good things we have, and it makes us feel good about ourselves.

I know that some people might think community service takes up too much time, but I think it's worth it. If we're only focused on ourselves, we'll miss out on a lot of opportunities to make a difference. I'd be happy to take on community service requirements because I believe it's an important part of being a student here.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]
texts.essays-claude-plain:
Dear Principal Davis,

I heard you are deciding if every student at our school has to do community service, and I wanted to write you before you decide. I think we should be required to do it, but only a small number of hours, and the school should count more things than just the official list.

The reason I say yes is that most kids will never try it unless somebody makes them. My friend Mia tutors second graders at Lincoln Elementary on Wednesdays, and she only started because her sister dragged her along. Now she talks about this one kid, Andre, who could barely read the word "through" in September and read a whole book to her in January. She says it is her favorite part of the week. If nobody had pushed her she would have just gone home and watched videos, and Andre would have had one less person helping him. There are probably fifty kids at our school who would end up loving something like that and will never find out on their own.

Also the town actually needs the help. Last spring my scout troop cleaned up the creek behind the middle school and we pulled out eleven tires, a shopping cart, and about nine bags of garbage in one Saturday morning. Eleven tires. Nobody was getting paid to do that and the creek was not going to clean itself. The food pantry on Main Street is another one, my mom volunteers there and she says they are always short of people on the days when donations come in. A few hundred students, even a few hours each, would be a real amount of help.

But I do understand the friends who say it takes too much time, and I do not think they are being lazy. My cousin Dev watches his two little brothers every day after school until his mom gets home at six thirty. He is already doing something for his family, and if the school told him he owed twenty more hours somewhere else, he would either fail the requirement or his brothers would sit alone. Some kids have jobs. Some kids have practice until dark. That is why I think the number should be small, like ten hours for the whole year, which is less than one hour a month, and everybody can find that.

My other suggestion is to let different things count. Babysitting for a neighbor who is sick, helping at your church or mosque, shoveling driveways for older people on our street in the winter, all of that is helping the community even if it is not on a sign up sheet. If the rule is too narrow, kids will just see it as another assignment to get out of instead of something they actually did for somebody.

So please require it, but keep it small and keep it fair.

Sincerely,
Jordan Alvarez
8th Grade

assignment.name: Community service
assignment.text:
Some of your friends perform community service. For example, some tutor elementary school children and others clean up litter. They think helping the community is very important. But other friends of yours think community service takes too much time away from what they need or want to do. 
Your principal is deciding whether to require all students to perform community service. 
Write a letter to your principal in which you take a position on whether students should be required to perform community service. Support your position with examples.
